source: Yesterday, we played this game with two numbers. We ended up

items.question: Yesterday, we played this game with two numbers. We ended up saying just ‘idli’ or ‘idli-vada’ and nobody said just ‘vada’! One of the numbers was 4. Oh, what could those numbers be!? Which of the following could be the other number: 2, 3, 5, 8, 10?
steps: Vada is said for multiples of the larger number, so every one of them must also be a multiple of the smaller number.
With 4 and 8, every multiple of 8 is a multiple of 4, so nobody says just vada.
With 2 and 4, every multiple of 4 is a multiple of 2, so that works too.
With 3, 5 or 10 someone says just vada: for 3 and 4 it is 4, for 4 and 5 it is 5, for 4 and 10 it is 10.
items.answer: 2 and 8 (the book names only 8).

videos.answer: 2 and 8 (the book names only 8).

items.question: Identify whether each statement is true or false. Explain. a. There is no prime number whose units digit is 4. b. A product of primes can also be prime. c. Prime numbers do not have any factors. d. All even numbers are composite numbers. e. 2 is a prime and so is the next number, 3. For every other prime, the next number is composite. a) There is no prime number whose units digit is 4. b) A product of primes can also be prime. c) Prime numbers do not have any factors. d) All even numbers are composite numbers. e) 2 is a prime and so is the next number, 3. For every other prime, the next number is composite.
steps: a) There is no prime number whose units digit is 4.: True; units digit 4 means even, and 2 is the only even prime.
b) A product of primes can also be prime.: False; a product of primes is composite.
c) Prime numbers do not have any factors.: False; a prime has exactly two factors, 1 and itself.
d) All even numbers are composite numbers.: False; all even numbers except 2 are composite.

e) 2 is a prime and so is the next number, 3. For every other prime, the next number is composite.: True; every other pair of consecutive numbers contains an even number greater than 2, which is composite.
items.answer: a True, b False, c False, d False, e True

videos.answer: a True, b False, c False, d False, e True

items.question: Can we list all the prime numbers from 1 to 100? Follow the steps: cross out 1; circle 2 and cross out its multiples; circle the next uncrossed number 3 and cross out its multiples; circle 5 and cross out its multiples; continue till all numbers are circled or crossed out.

source: Guna and Anshu started wondering how this simple method is a

items.question: Guna and Anshu started wondering how this simple method is able to find prime numbers! Think how this method works. Read the steps given above again and see what happens after each step is carried out.
steps: Each circled number has not been crossed out by any smaller circled number.
So it has no factor between 1 and itself: its only factors are 1 and itself.
A crossed-out number is a multiple of a smaller number, so it has more than two factors.
items.answer: Circled numbers have exactly two factors, so they are prime; crossed-out numbers have more, so they are composite.

source: Teacher asks: Are 56 and 63 co-prime? Anshu writes 56 = 14 ×

items.question: Teacher asks: Are 56 and 63 co-prime? Anshu writes 56 = 14 × 4 and 63 = 21 × 3 and says there are no common factors, so they are co-prime. Guna writes 56 = 7 × 8 and 63 = 9 × 7 and says 7 is a common factor, so they are not co-prime. Guna is right. But where did Anshu go wrong?
steps: 56 = 14 × 4 gives only some factors of 56 (14 and 4)
63 = 21 × 3 gives only some factors of 63
Other factorisations (56 = 7 × 8, 63 = 9 × 7) show 7 is common
So 56 and 63 are not co-prime
items.answer: Writing 56 = 14 × 4 only shows that 14 and 4 are factors of 56; it does not list all factors of 56 (same for 63). Anshu missed the common factor 7 because one factorisation does not reveal every factor.

videos.answer: Writing 56 = 14 × 4 only shows that 14 and 4 are factors of 56; it does not list all factors of 56 (same for 63). Anshu missed the common factor 7 because one factorisation does not reveal every factor.

source: Using this diagram, can you explain why 30 = 2 × 3 × 5, no m

items.question: Using this diagram, can you explain why 30 = 2 × 3 × 5, no matter which way you multiply 2, 3, and 5?
steps: The diagram is a cuboid made of unit cubes with 3 cubes along the front width, 2 along the height and 5 along the depth, so it has 2 × 3 × 5 = 30 cubes. Counting the same cubes layer by layer in any direction gives the same total, so the order of multiplication does not change the product. (Commutativity and associativity of multiplication, to be studied in a later class.)

source: 80 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 5 and 63 = 3 × 3 × 7. There are no comm

items.question: 80 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 5 and 63 = 3 × 3 × 7. There are no common prime factors. Can we conclude that they are co-prime? Suppose they have a common factor that is composite. Would the prime factors of this composite common factor appear in the prime factorisation of 80 and 63?
steps: Yes. A composite common factor would be a product of primes that divide both numbers, so its prime factors would appear in both prime factorisations.
